LECTURE 12 Stage 2: Tokenization & Data

Data Preprocessing Pipeline

Building the complete factory that transforms raw text into training-ready batches
45 min read Hands-on coding Intermediate

Putting It All Together

Over the past lectures, we have built each component of the input pipeline individually: a tokenizer to split text into tokens, a token embedding layer to convert IDs into dense vectors, and a positional embedding layer to encode word order. Now it is time to assemble them into a complete, end-to-end data pipeline that takes raw text and produces training-ready tensors.

Analogy: A Data Factory

Think of our pipeline as a data factory. Raw text goes in one end — messy, unstructured, full of irregularities. Through a series of processing stations (cleaning, tokenization, windowing, embedding), perfectly formatted training batches come out the other end, ready to feed the neural network. Each station does one job well, and together they form a reliable assembly line.

The End-to-End Pipeline Architecture

Step 1: Text Cleaning and Normalization

Before tokenization, we need to clean and normalize the raw text. Real-world text is messy: it contains inconsistent whitespace, unusual Unicode characters, HTML artifacts, and more. A good cleaning pipeline handles these issues systematically.

Python
import re

class TextCleaner:
 """Clean and normalize raw text for LLM training."""

 def __init__(self, lowercase=False, remove_urls=True,
 normalize_whitespace=True):
 self.lowercase = lowercase
 self.remove_urls = remove_urls
 self.normalize_whitespace = normalize_whitespace

 def clean(self, text):
 """Apply all cleaning steps in order."""
 # Step 1: Remove URLs
 if self.remove_urls:
 text = re.sub(r'https?://\\S+|www\\.\\S+', ' ', text)

 # Step 2: Normalize Unicode quotes and dashes
 replacements = {
 '\\u2018': "'", '\\u2019': "'", # Smart single quotes
 '\\u201c': '"', '\\u201d': '"', # Smart double quotes
 '\\u2014': ' -- ', '\\u2013': ' - ', # Em/en dashes
 '\\u2026': '...', # Ellipsis
 }
 for old, new in replacements.items():
 text = text.replace(old, new)

 # Step 3: Remove non-printable characters (keep newlines)
 text = re.sub(r'[^\\x20-\\x7E\
\\t]', '', text)

 # Step 4: Normalize whitespace
 if self.normalize_whitespace:
 text = re.sub(r'[ \\t]+', ' ', text) # Collapse spaces/tabs
 text = re.sub(r'\
{3,}', '\
\
', text) # Max 2 newlines
 text = text.strip()

 # Step 5: Optional lowercase
 if self.lowercase:
 text = text.lower()

 return text

# === Demo ===
cleaner = TextCleaner()

raw_text = """ The quick brown fox
jumps over https://example.com/page the lazy
dog. The cat sat on the mat.

Check out http://foo.bar for details.

This has weird spacing. """

print("=== BEFORE CLEANING ===")
print(repr(raw_text[:150]))

cleaned = cleaner.clean(raw_text)
print("\
=== AFTER CLEANING ===")
print(repr(cleaned))
print("\
=== Readable output ===")
print(cleaned)

# Show stats
print(f"\
--- Stats ---")
print(f"Original length: {len(raw_text)} chars")
print(f"Cleaned length: {len(cleaned)} chars")
print(f"Reduction: {(1 - len(cleaned)/len(raw_text))*100:.1f}%")
Cleaning Considerations for LLMs

For GPT-style models, we generally do not lowercase the text, because capitalization carries information (proper nouns, sentence beginnings, emphasis). The BPE tokenizer can handle mixed case. We also want to preserve paragraph structure (double newlines) since it provides useful context boundaries.

Step 2: The Sliding Window — Creating Training Pairs

LLMs are trained on a next-token prediction task: given a sequence of tokens, predict the next one. We create training examples using a sliding window over the tokenized text:

Sliding Window: Creating (Input, Target) Pairs

Full token sequence: [10, 24, 55, 88, 42, 17, 63, 91, 30, 75]

Context length = 4, Stride = 1:

Window 1: Input: [10, 24, 55, 88] Target: [24, 55, 88, 42]
Window 2: Input: [24, 55, 88, 42] Target: [55, 88, 42, 17]
Window 3: Input: [55, 88, 42, 17] Target: [88, 42, 17, 63]
Window 4: Input: [88, 42, 17, 63] Target: [42, 17, 63, 91]
Window 5: Input: [42, 17, 63, 91] Target: [17, 63, 91, 30]
Window 6: Input: [17, 63, 91, 30] Target: [63, 91, 30, 75]

Notice: Target is just Input shifted by 1 position!

Step 3: The GPTDataset Class

Now let us build the central class that ties everything together. The GPTDataset takes raw text, tokenizes it, and generates training pairs using the sliding window approach:

Python
import numpy as np
import re

class SimpleTokenizer:
 """Word-level tokenizer for demonstration."""
 def __init__(self):
 self.str_to_int = {}
 self.int_to_str = {}
 self.next_id = 0

 def build_vocab(self, text):
 """Build vocabulary from text."""
 words = text.lower().split()
 for w in words:
 if w not in self.str_to_int:
 self.str_to_int[w] = self.next_id
 self.int_to_str[self.next_id] = w
 self.next_id += 1

 def encode(self, text):
 return [self.str_to_int.get(w, 0) for w in text.lower().split()]

 def decode(self, ids):
 return " ".join(self.int_to_str.get(i, "?") for i in ids)

 @property
 def vocab_size(self):
 return len(self.str_to_int)

class GPTDataset:
 """
 Dataset that creates (input, target) pairs for GPT training.
 Combines tokenization + sliding window approach.
 """
 def __init__(self, text, tokenizer, context_length, stride=1):
 self.tokenizer = tokenizer
 self.context_length = context_length

 # Tokenize the entire text
 token_ids = tokenizer.encode(text)
 print(f"Total tokens in corpus: {len(token_ids)}")

 # Create input-target pairs using sliding window
 self.input_ids = []
 self.target_ids = []

 for i in range(0, len(token_ids) - context_length, stride):
 input_chunk = token_ids[i : i + context_length]
 target_chunk = token_ids[i + 1 : i + context_length + 1]
 self.input_ids.append(input_chunk)
 self.target_ids.append(target_chunk)

 print(f"Created {len(self.input_ids)} training examples")
 print(f"Context length: {context_length}")
 print(f"Stride: {stride}")

 def __len__(self):
 return len(self.input_ids)

 def __getitem__(self, idx):
 return np.array(self.input_ids[idx]), np.array(self.target_ids[idx])

# === Build and test the dataset ===
text = """the cat sat on the mat the dog ran to the house
the big cat sat on a small mat the brown dog ran to a big house
the small cat sat on the big mat the cat and the dog ran home"""

tokenizer = SimpleTokenizer()
tokenizer.build_vocab(text)
print(f"Vocabulary size: {tokenizer.vocab_size}")
print(f"Vocabulary: {dict(list(tokenizer.str_to_int.items())[:15])}...")

context_length = 4
dataset = GPTDataset(text, tokenizer, context_length, stride=2)

# Show some examples
print(f"\
=== Sample Training Pairs ===")
for i in range(min(5, len(dataset))):
 inp, tgt = dataset[i]
 inp_words = tokenizer.decode(inp)
 tgt_words = tokenizer.decode(tgt)
 print(f" Example {i}:")
 print(f" Input: {inp} -> '{inp_words}'")
 print(f" Target: {tgt} -> '{tgt_words}'")

Step 4: Batch Processing

Neural networks train more efficiently on batches of data rather than one example at a time. A batch groups multiple training examples together, enabling parallel computation on GPUs and providing more stable gradient estimates.

Python
import numpy as np

class DataLoader:
 """
 Simple data loader that creates batches from a dataset.
 Similar to PyTorch's DataLoader.\
 """
 def __init__(self, dataset, batch_size, shuffle=True):
 self.dataset = dataset
 self.batch_size = batch_size
 self.shuffle = shuffle

 def __iter__(self):
 indices = list(range(len(self.dataset)))
 if self.shuffle:
 np.random.shuffle(indices)

 for start in range(0, len(indices), self.batch_size):
 batch_indices = indices[start : start + self.batch_size]
 batch_inputs = []
 batch_targets = []
 for idx in batch_indices:
 inp, tgt = self.dataset[idx]
 batch_inputs.append(inp)
 batch_targets.append(tgt)
 yield np.array(batch_inputs), np.array(batch_targets)

 def __len__(self):
 return (len(self.dataset) + self.batch_size - 1) // self.batch_size

Step 5: The Complete Pipeline

Now let us assemble everything into one cohesive pipeline that goes from raw text all the way to embedded, training-ready tensors:

Python
import numpy as np
import re

# ===== COMPONENT 1: Text Cleaner =====
class TextCleaner:
 def clean(self, text):
 text = re.sub(r'https?://\\S+', ' ', text)
 text = re.sub(r'[ \\t]+', ' ', text)
 return text.strip()

# ===== COMPONENT 2: Tokenizer =====
class SimpleTokenizer:
 def __init__(self):
 self.str_to_int = {}
 self.int_to_str = {}
 self.next_id = 0
 def build_vocab(self, text):
 for w in text.lower().split():
 if w not in self.str_to_int:
 self.str_to_int[w] = self.next_id
 self.int_to_str[self.next_id] = w
 self.next_id += 1
 def encode(self, text):
 return [self.str_to_int.get(w, 0) for w in text.lower().split()]
 def decode(self, ids):
 return " ".join(self.int_to_str.get(i, "?") for i in ids)
 @property
 def vocab_size(self):
 return len(self.str_to_int)

# ===== COMPONENT 3: Embedding =====
class Embedding:
 def __init__(self, num_embeddings, embedding_dim):
 scale = np.sqrt(1.0 / embedding_dim)
 self.weight = np.random.randn(num_embeddings, embedding_dim) * scale
 def forward(self, ids):
 return self.weight[np.array(ids)]

# ===== COMPONENT 4: Dataset =====
class GPTDataset:
 def __init__(self, token_ids, context_length, stride):
 self.input_ids = []
 self.target_ids = []
 for i in range(0, len(token_ids) - context_length, stride):
 self.input_ids.append(token_ids[i : i + context_length])
 self.target_ids.append(token_ids[i + 1 : i + context_length + 1])
 def __len__(self):
 return len(self.input_ids)
 def __getitem__(self, idx):
 return np.array(self.input_ids[idx]), np.array(self.target_ids[idx])

# ===== COMPONENT 5: Data Loader =====
class DataLoader:
 def __init__(self, dataset, batch_size, shuffle=True):
 self.dataset = dataset
 self.batch_size = batch_size
 self.shuffle = shuffle
 def __iter__(self):
 indices = list(range(len(self.dataset)))
 if self.shuffle:
 np.random.shuffle(indices)
 for start in range(0, len(indices), self.batch_size):
 batch_idx = indices[start : start + self.batch_size]
 inputs = np.array([self.dataset[i][0] for i in batch_idx])
 targets = np.array([self.dataset[i][1] for i in batch_idx])
 yield inputs, targets

# ===== THE COMPLETE PIPELINE =====
class GPTDataPipeline:
 """End-to-end pipeline: raw text -> training-ready embedded batches."""

 def __init__(self, embed_dim=8, context_length=4,
 batch_size=2, stride=2):
 self.embed_dim = embed_dim
 self.context_length = context_length
 self.batch_size = batch_size
 self.stride = stride
 self.cleaner = TextCleaner()
 self.tokenizer = SimpleTokenizer()

 def prepare(self, raw_text):
 """Build vocabulary and create dataset from raw text."""
 # Step 1: Clean
 self.cleaned_text = self.cleaner.clean(raw_text)
 print(f"[1/5] Cleaned text: {len(self.cleaned_text)} chars")

 # Step 2: Build vocab and tokenize
 self.tokenizer.build_vocab(self.cleaned_text)
 self.token_ids = self.tokenizer.encode(self.cleaned_text)
 print(f"[2/5] Tokenized: {len(self.token_ids)} tokens, "
 f"vocab size: {self.tokenizer.vocab_size}")

 # Step 3: Create dataset with sliding window
 self.dataset = GPTDataset(
 self.token_ids, self.context_length, self.stride
 )
 print(f"[3/5] Dataset: {len(self.dataset)} training examples")

 # Step 4: Create data loader
 self.loader = DataLoader(
 self.dataset, self.batch_size, shuffle=False
 )
 print(f"[4/5] DataLoader: batch_size={self.batch_size}")

 # Step 5: Initialize embeddings
 self.token_emb = Embedding(self.tokenizer.vocab_size, self.embed_dim)
 self.pos_emb = Embedding(self.context_length, self.embed_dim)
 print(f"[5/5] Embeddings: token({self.tokenizer.vocab_size}, "
 f"{self.embed_dim}), pos({self.context_length}, {self.embed_dim})")

 return self

 def get_batch_embeddings(self, input_ids):
 """Convert a batch of token IDs to embedded representations."""
 batch_size, seq_len = input_ids.shape
 pos_ids = list(range(seq_len))

 # Get position embeddings (same for all items in batch)
 pos_embeddings = self.pos_emb.forward(pos_ids) # (seq_len, embed_dim)

 # Process each item in the batch
 results = []
 for i in range(batch_size):
 tok_embeddings = self.token_emb.forward(input_ids[i])
 combined = tok_embeddings + pos_embeddings
 results.append(combined)

 return np.array(results) # (batch_size, seq_len, embed_dim)


# ===== RUN THE COMPLETE PIPELINE =====
np.random.seed(42)

raw_text = """
The cat sat on the mat. The dog ran to the house.
The big cat sat on a small mat.
The brown dog ran to a big house.
The small cat sat on the big mat.
The cat and the dog ran home together.
"""

print("=" * 55)
print(" COMPLETE GPT DATA PIPELINE")
print("=" * 55)

pipeline = GPTDataPipeline(
 embed_dim=8,
 context_length=4,
 batch_size=2,
 stride=2
)
pipeline.prepare(raw_text)

print(f"\
{'=' * 55}")
print(" PROCESSING BATCHES")
print("=" * 55)

for batch_num, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(pipeline.loader):
 embeddings = pipeline.get_batch_embeddings(inputs)

 print(f"\
Batch {batch_num}:")
 print(f" Raw input IDs: shape {inputs.shape}")
 print(f" Target IDs: shape {targets.shape}")
 print(f" Embedded inputs: shape {embeddings.shape}")

 # Show detail for first batch
 if batch_num == 0:
 print(f"\
 --- Detail for first example in batch ---")
 words_in = [pipeline.tokenizer.int_to_str.get(i, "?")
 for i in inputs[0]]
 words_tgt = [pipeline.tokenizer.int_to_str.get(i, "?")
 for i in targets[0]]
 print(f" Input words: {words_in}")
 print(f" Target words: {words_tgt}")
 print(f" Embedding[0]: {embeddings[0][0].round(3)}")

 if batch_num >= 3:
 print(" ... (remaining batches omitted)")
 break

print(f"\
{'=' * 55}")
print(" PIPELINE SUMMARY")
print("=" * 55)
print(f" Raw text chars: {len(raw_text)}")
print(f" Cleaned text chars: {len(pipeline.cleaned_text)}")
print(f" Total tokens: {len(pipeline.token_ids)}")
print(f" Vocabulary size: {pipeline.tokenizer.vocab_size}")
print(f" Training examples: {len(pipeline.dataset)}")
print(f" Context length: {pipeline.context_length}")
print(f" Embedding dimension: {pipeline.embed_dim}")
print(f" Output tensor shape: (batch, {pipeline.context_length}, "
 f"{pipeline.embed_dim})")

Memory Efficiency Considerations

When working with large text corpora (billions of tokens), memory becomes a critical concern. Here are key strategies used in practice:

Lazy Loading

Do not load the entire corpus into memory. Read and tokenize chunks on demand, or pre-tokenize and memory-map the file.

Stride Control

Using stride = context_length (non-overlapping windows) reduces the dataset size dramatically compared to stride = 1.

Token Type

Store token IDs as int16 or int32 instead of int64. With a 50K vocabulary, 16-bit integers are sufficient and halve memory usage.

Packing

Pack multiple shorter documents into a single training sequence (separated by special tokens) to avoid wasting padding space.

Connection to the Book

Chapter 2 of "Build an LLM from Scratch" implements essentially this same pipeline using PyTorch's Dataset and DataLoader classes. Our pure-Python version follows the same logic: tokenize, create sliding window pairs, batch, and embed. When you move to PyTorch, the main difference is that embedding lookups and batching are handled by optimized GPU-aware code.

Data Augmentation for Text (Brief Overview)

While less common than in computer vision, there are some data augmentation techniques for text:

Technique Description Use in LLM Training
Random masking Replace random tokens with a mask token Used in BERT, not GPT
Document shuffling Randomize the order of documents in each epoch Standard practice
Token dropout Randomly remove tokens during training Sometimes used as regularization
Context length variation Use varying context lengths during training Can improve generalization
Stride vs. Dataset Size Trade-off

With stride=1 on a text of 1 million tokens and context_length=1024, you get ~999,000 training examples. With stride=1024 (non-overlapping), you get only ~976 examples. More overlap means more training data but also more redundancy and higher memory usage. GPT-style training typically uses stride = context_length (non-overlapping) for efficiency.

Preview: Stage 3 — The Attention Mechanism

With our data pipeline complete, we are ready for the most exciting part of the Transformer architecture: the attention mechanism. Here is what is coming in Stage 3:

Lecture 13: Self-Attention Intuition

How tokens "look at" other tokens to understand context. Why "bank" means different things in "river bank" vs. "bank account."

Când lucrați cu corpusuri mari de text (miliarde de token-uri), memoria devine o preocupare critică. Iată strategiile cheie utilizate în practică:

Încărcare la cerere

Nu încărcați întregul corpus în memorie. Citiți și tokenizați fragmente la cerere, sau pre-tokenizați și mapați fișierul în memorie.

Controlul pasului

Folosirea stride = context_length (ferestre nesuprapuse) reduce dramatic dimensiunea setului de date comparativ cu stride = 1.

Tipul token-ului

Stocați ID-urile token-urilor ca int16 sau int32 în loc de int64. Cu un vocabular de 50K, întregii pe 16 biți sunt suficienți și înjumătățesc utilizarea memoriei.

Împachetare

Împachetați mai multe documente mai scurte într-o singură secvență de antrenament (separate prin token-uri speciale) pentru a evita risipirea spațiului de padding.

Βημα 1: Καθαρισμος και Κανονικοποιηση Κειμενου

Πριν το tokenization, πρεπει να καθαρισουμε και κανονικοποιησουμε το ακατεργαστο κειμενο. Το κειμενο του πραγματικου κοσμου ειναι ακαταστατο: περιεχει ασυνεπη κενα, ασυνηθιστους χαρακτηρες Unicode, αρτεφακτα HTML και αλλα. Ενας καλος αγωγος καθαρισμου αντιμετωπιζει αυτα τα ζητηματα συστηματικα.

class TextCleaner:
 """Clean and normalize raw text for LLM training."""

 def __init__(self, lowercase=False, remove_urls=True,
 normalize_whitespace=True):
 self.lowercase = lowercase
 self.remove_urls = remove_urls
 self.normalize_whitespace = normalize_whitespace

 def clean(self, text):
 """Apply all cleaning steps in order."""
 # Step 1: Remove URLs
 if self.remove_urls:
 text = re.sub(r'https?://\\S+|www\\.\\S+', ' ', text)

 # Step 2: Normalize Unicode quotes and dashes
 replacements = {
 '\\u2018': "'", '\\u2019': "'", # Smart single quotes
 '\\u201c': '"', '\\u201d': '"', # Smart double quotes
 '\\u2014': ' -- ', '\\u2013': ' - ', # Em/en dashes
 '\\u2026': '...', # Ellipsis
 }
 for old, new in replacements.items():
 text = text.replace(old, new)

 # Step 3: Remove non-printable characters (keep newlines)
 text = re.sub(r'[^\\x20-\\x7E\
\\t]', '', text)

 # Step 4: Normalize whitespace
 if self.normalize_whitespace:
 text = re.sub(r'[ \\t]+', ' ', text) # Collapse spaces/tabs
 text = re.sub(r'\
{3,}', '\
\
', text) # Max 2 newlines
 text = text.strip()

 # Step 5: Optional lowercase
 if self.lowercase:
 text = text.lower()

 return text

import numpy as np
import re

class SimpleTokenizer:
 """Word-level tokenizer for demonstration."""
 def __init__(self):
 self.str_to_int = {}
 self.int_to_str = {}
 self.next_id = 0

 def build_vocab(self, text):
 """Build vocabulary from text."""
 words = text.lower().split()
 for w in words:
 if w not in self.str_to_int:
 self.str_to_int[w] = self.next_id
 self.int_to_str[self.next_id] = w
 self.next_id += 1

 def encode(self, text):
 return [self.str_to_int.get(w, 0) for w in text.lower().split()]

 def decode(self, ids):
 return " ".join(self.int_to_str.get(i, "?") for i in ids)

 @property
 def vocab_size(self):
 return len(self.str_to_int)

class GPTDataset:
 """
 Dataset that creates (input, target) pairs for GPT training.
 Combines tokenization + sliding window approach.
 """
 def __init__(self, text, tokenizer, context_length, stride=1):
 self.tokenizer = tokenizer
 self.context_length = context_length

 # Tokenize the entire text
 token_ids = tokenizer.encode(text)
 print(f"Total tokens in corpus: {len(token_ids)}")

 # Create input-target pairs using sliding window
 self.input_ids = []
 self.target_ids = []

 for i in range(0, len(token_ids) - context_length, stride):
 input_chunk = token_ids[i : i + context_length]
 target_chunk = token_ids[i + 1 : i + context_length + 1]
 self.input_ids.append(input_chunk)
 self.target_ids.append(target_chunk)

 print(f"Created {len(self.input_ids)} training examples")
 print(f"Context length: {context_length}")
 print(f"Stride: {stride}")

 def __len__(self):
 return len(self.input_ids)

 def __getitem__(self, idx):
 return np.array(self.input_ids[idx]), np.array(self.target_ids[idx])

class GPTDataPipeline:
 """End-to-end pipeline: raw text -> training-ready embedded batches."""

 def __init__(self, embed_dim=8, context_length=4,
 batch_size=2, stride=2):
 self.embed_dim = embed_dim
 self.context_length = context_length
 self.batch_size = batch_size
 self.stride = stride
 self.cleaner = TextCleaner()
 self.tokenizer = SimpleTokenizer()

 def prepare(self, raw_text):
 """Build vocabulary and create dataset from raw text."""
 # Step 1: Clean
 self.cleaned_text = self.cleaner.clean(raw_text)
 print(f"[1/5] Cleaned text: {len(self.cleaned_text)} chars")

 # Step 2: Build vocab and tokenize
 self.tokenizer.build_vocab(self.cleaned_text)
 self.token_ids = self.tokenizer.encode(self.cleaned_text)
 print(f"[2/5] Tokenized: {len(self.token_ids)} tokens, "
 f"vocab size: {self.tokenizer.vocab_size}")

 # Step 3: Create dataset with sliding window
 self.dataset = GPTDataset(
 self.token_ids, self.context_length, self.stride
 )
 print(f"[3/5] Dataset: {len(self.dataset)} training examples")

 # Step 4: Create data loader
 self.loader = DataLoader(
 self.dataset, self.batch_size, shuffle=False
 )
 print(f"[4/5] DataLoader: batch_size={self.batch_size}")

 # Step 5: Initialize embeddings
 self.token_emb = Embedding(self.tokenizer.vocab_size, self.embed_dim)
 self.pos_emb = Embedding(self.context_length, self.embed_dim)
 print(f"[5/5] Embeddings: token({self.tokenizer.vocab_size}, "
 f"{self.embed_dim}), pos({self.context_length}, {self.embed_dim})")

 return self

 def get_batch_embeddings(self, input_ids):
 """Convert a batch of token IDs to embedded representations."""
 batch_size, seq_len = input_ids.shape
 pos_ids = list(range(seq_len))

 # Get position embeddings (same for all items in batch)
 pos_embeddings = self.pos_emb.forward(pos_ids) # (seq_len, embed_dim)

 # Process each item in the batch
 results = []
 for i in range(batch_size):
 tok_embeddings = self.token_emb.forward(input_ids[i])
 combined = tok_embeddings + pos_embeddings
 results.append(combined)

 return np.array(results) # (batch_size, seq_len, embed_dim)

Σκεψεις Αποδοτικοτητας Μνημης

Οταν δουλευουμε με μεγαλα σωματα κειμενου (δισεκατομμυρια tokens), η μνημη γινεται κρισιμο ζητημα. Ακολουθουν βασικες στρατηγικες που χρησιμοποιουνται στην πραξη:

Τεμπελης Φορτωση

Μην φορτωνετε ολοκληρο το σωμα κειμενου στη μνημη. Διαβαστε και καντε tokenize κομματια κατα απαιτηση, η καντε προ-tokenize και memory-map το αρχειο.

Ελεγχος Stride

Χρησιμοποιωντας stride = context_length (μη επικαλυπτομενα παραθυρα) μειωνει το μεγεθος του dataset δραματικα σε σχεση με stride = 1.

Τυπος Token

Αποθηκευστε τα token IDs ως int16 η int32 αντι για int64. Με λεξιλογιο 50K, οι ακεραιοι 16-bit ειναι αρκετοι και μειωνουν τη χρηση μνημης στο μισο.

Συσκευασια

Συσκευαστε πολλα συντομοτερα εγγραφα σε μια μοναδικη ακολουθια εκπαιδευσης (χωρισμενα με ειδικα tokens) για να αποφυγετε σπαταλη χωρου padding.

Συνδεση με το Βιβλιο

Το Κεφαλαιο 2 του "Build an LLM from Scratch" υλοποιει ουσιαστικα τον ιδιο αγωγο χρησιμοποιωντας τις κλασεις Dataset και DataLoader του PyTorch. Η υλοποιηση μας σε καθαρη Python ακολουθει την ιδια λογικη: tokenize, δημιουργια ζευγων συρομενου παραθυρου, παρτιδοποιηση και embedding. Οταν μεταβειτε στο PyTorch, η κυρια διαφορα ειναι οτι οι αναζητησεις embedding και η παρτιδοποιηση γινονται απο βελτιστοποιημενο κωδικα που γνωριζει GPU.

Επαυξηση Δεδομενων για Κειμενο (Συντομη Επισκοπηση)

Αν και λιγοτερο συνηθισμενη απο &omicron,τι στην υπολογιστικη οραση, υπαρχουν καποιες τεχνικες επαυξησης δεδομενων για κειμενο:

Τεχνικη Περιγραφη Χρηση στην Εκπαιδευση LLM
Τυχαια καλυψη Αντικατασταση τυχαιων tokens με mask token Χρησιμοποιειται στο BERT, οχι στο GPT
Ανακατευθυνση εγγραφων Τυχαιοποιηση της σειρας εγγραφων σε καθε epoch Καθιερωμενη πρακτικη
Token dropout Τυχαια αφαιρεση tokens κατα την εκπαιδευση Χρησιμοποιειται καπου ως κανονικοποιηση
Μεταβολη μηκους συμφραζομενων Χρηση μεταβαλλομενων μηκων συμφραζομενων κατα την εκπαιδευση Μπορει να βελτιωσει τη γενικευση
Αντισταθμιση Stride εναντιον Μεγεθους Dataset

Με stride=1 σε κειμενο 1 εκατομμυριου tokens και context_length=1024, παιρνετε ~999.000 παραδειγματα εκπαιδευσης. Με stride=1024 (μη επικαλυπτομενα), παιρνετε μονο ~976 παραδειγματα. Περισσοτερη επικαλυψη σημαινει περισσοτερα δεδομενα εκπαιδευσης αλλα και περισσοτερη πλεονασματικοτητα και υψηλοτερη χρηση μνημης. Η εκπαιδευση στυλ GPT συνηθως χρησιμοποιει stride = context_length (μη επικαλυπτομενα) για αποδοτικοτητα.

Überlegungen zur Speichereffizienz

Bei der Arbeit mit großen Textkorpora (Milliarden von Tokens) wird der Speicher zu einem kritischen Anliegen. Hier sind einige wichtige Strategien aus der Praxis:

Lazy Loading

Laden Sie nicht das gesamte Korpus in den Speicher. Lesen und tokenisieren Sie Abschnitte bei Bedarf, oder tokenisieren Sie vorab und mappen Sie die Datei per Memory-Mapping.

Stride-Kontrolle

Die Verwendung von stride = context_length (nicht überlappende Fenster) reduziert die Datensatzgröße im Vergleich zu stride = 1 drastisch.

Token-Typ

Speichern Sie Token-IDs als int16 oder int32 statt int64. Bei einem Vokabular von 50.000 sind 16-Bit-Ganzzahlen ausreichend und halbieren den Speicherverbrauch.

Packing

Packen Sie mehrere kürzere Dokumente in eine einzige Trainingssequenz (getrennt durch Spezial-Tokens), um verschwendeten Padding-Platz zu vermeiden.

Bezug zum Buch

Kapitel 2 von "Build an LLM from Scratch" implementiert im Wesentlichen dieselbe Pipeline mithilfe der Klassen Dataset und DataLoader von PyTorch. Unsere reine Python-Version folgt derselben Logik: tokenisieren, gleitende Fensterpaare erstellen, batchen und einbetten. Wenn Sie zu PyTorch wechseln, besteht der Hauptunterschied darin, dass Embedding-Lookups und Batching von optimiertem, GPU-fähigem Code übernommen werden.

Datenaugmentierung für Text (kurzer Überblick)

Obwohl weniger verbreitet als im Bereich Computer Vision, gibt es einige Techniken zur Datenaugmentierung für Text:

Technik Beschreibung Einsatz beim LLM-Training
Zufälliges Maskieren Ersetzt zufällige Tokens durch ein Masken-Token Wird bei BERT verwendet, nicht bei GPT
Dokumenten-Shuffling Randomisiert die Reihenfolge der Dokumente in jeder Epoche Gängige Praxis
Token-Dropout Entfernt während des Trainings zufällig Tokens Wird manchmal als Regularisierung verwendet
Variation der Kontextlänge Verwendet während des Trainings unterschiedliche Kontextlängen Kann die Generalisierung verbessern
Kompromiss zwischen Stride und Datensatzgröße

Chargement paresseux

Ne chargez pas l'intégralité du corpus en mémoire. Lisez et tokenisez des blocs à la demande, ou pré-tokenisez et mappez le fichier en mémoire (memory-map).

Contrôle du stride

Utiliser stride = context_length (fenêtres non chevauchantes) réduit considérablement la taille du jeu de données par rapport à stride = 1.

Type de token

Stockez les ID de tokens en int16 ou int32 plutôt qu'en int64. Avec un vocabulaire de 50K, des entiers 16 bits suffisent et réduisent de moitié l'utilisation de la mémoire.

Empaquetage

Empaquetez plusieurs documents plus courts dans une seule séquence d'entraînement (séparés par des tokens spéciaux) pour éviter de gaspiller de l'espace de padding.

import re

class SimpleTokenizer:
 """Word-level tokenizer for demonstration."""
 def __init__(self):
 self.str_to_int = {}
 self.int_to_str = {}
 self.next_id = 0

 def build_vocab(self, text):
 """Build vocabulary from text."""
 words = text.lower().split()
 for w in words:
 if w not in self.str_to_int:
 self.str_to_int[w] = self.next_id
 self.int_to_str[self.next_id] = w
 self.next_id += 1

 def encode(self, text):
 return [self.str_to_int.get(w, 0) for w in text.lower().split()]

 def decode(self, ids):
 return " ".join(self.int_to_str.get(i, "?") for i in ids)

 @property

 return len(self.str_to_int)

class GPTDataset:
 """
 Dataset that creates (input, target) pairs for GPT training.
 Combines tokenization + sliding window approach.

 self.context_length = context_length

 # Create input-target pairs using sliding window
 self.input_ids = []
 self.target_ids = []

 self.target_ids.append(target_chunk)

 def __len__(self):

Considerazioni sull'Efficienza della Memoria

Quando si lavora con corpora di testo di grandi dimensioni (miliardi di token), la memoria diventa una preoccupazione critica. Ecco le strategie chiave utilizzate nella pratica:

Caricamento Pigro

Non caricate l'intero corpus in memoria. Leggete e tokenizzate blocchi di testo su richiesta, oppure pre-tokenizzate e mappate il file in memoria.

Controllo del Passo

Utilizzare stride = context_length (finestre non sovrapposte) riduce drasticamente la dimensione del dataset rispetto a stride = 1.

Tipo di Token

Memorizzate gli ID dei token come int16 o int32 invece di int64. Con un vocabolario di 50K, gli interi a 16 bit sono sufficienti e dimezzano l'utilizzo della memoria.

Impacchettamento

Impacchettate più documenti brevi in un'unica sequenza di addestramento (separati da token speciali) per evitare di sprecare spazio di padding.

Collegamento con il Libro

Il capitolo 2 di "Build an LLM from Scratch" implementa essenzialmente questa stessa pipeline utilizzando le classi Dataset e DataLoader di PyTorch. La nostra versione in puro Python segue la stessa logica: tokenizzare, creare coppie con finestra scorrevole, raggruppare in batch ed effettuare l'embedding. Quando passerete a PyTorch, la differenza principale è che le ricerche di embedding e la creazione dei batch sono gestite da codice ottimizzato e compatibile con le GPU.

Compromesso tra Passo (Stride) e Dimensione del Dataset

Con stride=1 su un testo di 1 milione di token e context_length=1024, si ottengono circa 999.000 esempi di addestramento. Con stride=1024 (senza sovrapposizione), si ottengono solo circa 976 esempi. Con la nostra pipeline di dati completa, siamo pronti per la parte più entusiasmante dell'architettura Transformer: il meccanismo di attenzione. Ecco cosa ci aspetta nella Fase 3:

Come i token "osservano" altri token per comprendere il contesto. Perché "bank" significa cose diverse in "river bank" vs. "bank account."

Le matrici Query, Key, Value. L'attenzione a prodotto scalare scalato (scaled dot-product attention). La matrice dei punteggi di attenzione e la softmax.

 self.int_to_str = {}

اعتبارات كفاءة الذاكرة

عند العمل مع مدونات نصية ضخمة (مليارات الرموز)، تصبح الذاكرة مصدر قلق بالغ الأهمية. فيما يلي أهم الاستراتيجيات المستخدمة عمليًا:

التحميل الكسول

لا تُحمّل المدونة النصية بأكملها في الذاكرة. اقرأ الأجزاء ورمّزها عند الحاجة، أو رمّز الملف مسبقًا واربطه بالذاكرة (memory-map).

التحكم في الخطوة

يؤدي استخدام stride = context_length (نوافذ غير متداخلة) إلى تقليص حجم مجموعة البيانات بشكل كبير مقارنةً بـ stride = 1.

نوع بيانات الرمز

خزّن معرّفات الرموز باستخدام int16 أو int32 بدلاً من int64. مع مفردات بحجم 50 ألفًا، تكون الأعداد الصحيحة ذات 16 بت كافية وتُخفّض استخدام الذاكرة إلى النصف.

الحزم

احزم عدة مستندات أقصر في تسلسل تدريب واحد (مفصولة برموز خاصة) لتجنب إهدار مساحة الحشو.

الصلة بالكتاب

ينفّذ الفصل الثاني من كتاب "Build an LLM from Scratch" أساسًا خط المعالجة نفسه باستخدام صنفَي Dataset وDataLoader في PyTorch. تتبع نسختنا المكتوبة بلغة Python الخالصة المنطق ذاته: الترميز، إنشاء أزواج النافذة المنزلقة، التجميع في دفعات، والتضمين. وعند الانتقال إلى PyTorch، يكمن الفرق الرئيسي في أن عمليات البحث عن التضمينات والتجميع في دفعات تُدار بواسطة كود مُحسَّن يستفيد من وحدة معالجة الرسومات (GPU).

زيادة البيانات النصية (نظرة موجزة)

على الرغم من أنها أقل شيوعًا مقارنةً برؤية الحاسوب، توجد بعض تقنيات زيادة البيانات الخاصة بالنصوص:

التقنية الوصف الاستخدام في تدريب نماذج اللغة الكبيرة
الإخفاء العشوائي استبدال رموز عشوائية برمز إخفاء يُستخدم في BERT، وليس في GPT
خلط المستندات عشوائية ترتيب المستندات في كل حقبة تدريب (epoch) ممارسة معيارية
إسقاط الرموز إزالة رموز عشوائيًا أثناء التدريب يُستخدم أحيانًا كوسيلة للتسوية (regularization)
تنويع طول السياق استخدام أطوال سياق متفاوتة أثناء التدريب قد يُحسّن قدرة التعميم
المفاضلة بين الخطوة (Stride) وحجم مجموعة البيانات

باستخدام stride=1 على نص من مليون رمز وcontext_length=1024، تحصل على نحو 999,000 مثال تدريب. أما باستخدام stride=1024 (بلا تداخل)، فلا تحصل إلا على نحو 976 مثالًا فقط. التداخل الأكبر يعني بيانات تدريب أكثر، لكنه يعني أيضًا تكرارًا أكبر واستخدامًا أعلى للذاكرة. يستخدم التدريب بأسلوب GPT عادةً stride = context_length (بلا تداخل) من أجل الكفاءة.

المحاضرة 13: الحدس وراء الانتباه الذاتي
